items.title: 21.11 Global Climate and Energy Transfer from the Sun

source_refs.note: Topic 21.11 with boxes (PDF 179-181); Figs 21.12 (empty-box diagram) and 21.13 redrawn. The check question is added; answer needs review.

blocks.text: Energy received from the Sun plays an important role in changes in the global climate. This section describes how the energy received from the Sun is distributed on Earth, and how uneven heating between the equator and the poles produces atmospheric changes.

blocks.title: Earth's energy budget
blocks.text: The Earth's energy budget is the balance between the solar energy absorbed by the Earth and the energy it radiates back into space.

It measures how much solar energy reaches the Earth and how much is lost to space by reflection and emission. When the Earth is colder, more ice and snow cover the surface; ice and snow are bright and reflect a lot of sunlight back into space, which makes the Earth cooler still. When the Earth warms, ice and snow melt, exposing darker land and ocean, which absorb more sunlight and reflect less, so the Earth warms further. The energy coming in from the Sun is balanced by the energy going out as infrared (heat) radiation (Fig 21.12). While this balance is maintained, the Earth's temperature stays constant. But greenhouse gases trap infrared radiation, preventing it from escaping into space; as a result the Earth is warming, a problem known as global warming.

blocks.alt: The Sun sends sunlight down through the atmosphere and clouds to the Earth's surface; an arrow shows about 30 per cent reflected back to space by clouds, ice and deserts. Wavy red arrows show infrared rising from the surface; some passes on to space and purple arrows show greenhouse gases sending some back down. A note states that energy absorbed (about 70 per cent of sunlight) equals infrared radiated to space, and trapping more infrared warms the Earth.
blocks.caption: Earth's energy budget (original diagram after Fig 21.12).
blocks.long_description: Sunlight comes in mostly as visible light; the Earth sends energy out as infrared. If greenhouse gases return more of that infrared, the outgoing flow falls below the incoming flow and the Earth warms until a new balance is reached.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: The Earth absorbs only about 70 per cent of the Sun's energy that reaches it; the rest is reflected back into space by clouds, ice and desert surfaces. A 1 per cent imbalance in this budget can lead to major global temperature shifts.
2. Energy imbalance between the poles and the equator

The Earth's climate system is shaped by the uneven distribution of solar energy over its surface (Fig 21.13). The equator receives direct, intense sunlight, so warm air rises there and forms low-pressure zones, while the poles receive slanted, weaker sunlight, giving cold sinking air and high-pressure zones. This energy imbalance drives the global atmospheric circulation, creating wind patterns such as the trade winds near the equator, the westerlies in mid-latitudes and the polar easterlies near the poles. These winds, together with ocean currents, redistribute heat around the world. Human-induced greenhouse gas emissions are disrupting this natural balance, intensifying global warming and changing weather patterns.

blocks.alt: Left: sunlight arriving as parallel arrows strikes the Earth; at the equator it hits directly and is concentrated (hotter), near the poles it strikes at a low angle and is spread out (cooler). Right: a globe with the equator dashed; air moving north from the equator curves to the right and air moving south curves to the left; the Earth turns from west to east; specific angular momentum L = rv is conserved.
blocks.caption: Uneven heating and the Coriolis deflection (original diagram after Fig 21.13).
blocks.long_description: The same beam of sunlight is spread over a larger area near the poles than at the equator, so the poles get less energy per square metre. The resulting flow of air is turned sideways by the Earth's rotation.
